faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other such that, from Earth's viewpoint, one star periodically passes in front of the other. When this happens, the combined brightness of the system dips. By studying these brightness dips in a light curve, astronomers can measure the orbital period and relative sizes of the stars.
faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?

faqs.answer: A candidate is a target that passed statistical vetting and novelty cross-checking but has not yet been checked at the pixel level. A confirmed candidate (on this site) is one that passed the automated pixel-level check, meaning the eclipse signal comes from the target star itself and not from contamination by a nearby star. 'Confirmed' here refers only to this automated vetting step and does not imply scientific verification or professional follow-up.
faqs.question: What's the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' candidate on this site?

faqs.answer: The ML score is a logistic regression model trained on 1,058 labeled examples. It serves as a second opinion on the quality of a candidate, and outperforms the rule-based pipeline. However, it is not used to decide which candidates get the pixel-level check - all novel candidates are checked. The score is provided for reference only and is not used to guide any downstream work.
faqs.question: What is the machine learning score on candidate pages?

faqs.answer: Each candidate undergoes an automated pixel-level check that examines whether the eclipse signal originates from the target star itself or from a nearby star whose light may have contaminated the photometry. This check is fully automated and requires no human review. Candidates that pass this test are confirmed as on-target.
faqs.question: How does Star Vetter check whether a candidate is real?

faqs.answer: Star Vetter compares the eclipse depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses. If these depths differ significantly, it suggests the measured period may be an alias of the true period. Such candidates are flagged with a note on their individual page, leaving open the possibility that the true period is a harmonic or subharmonic of the measured one.
faqs.question: What happens if the period looks aliased?

faqs.answer: Being listed on this site is the end of what the Star Vetter pipeline itself does. The site makes candidates and their measured periods and eclipse depths publicly available, but this project does not conduct follow-up observations, add candidates to official catalogs, or perform spectroscopic characterization. Any further study is the work of other researchers.
faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it's listed on Star Vetter?

narrative: Star Vetter automatically vets candidate eclipsing binary stars found in TESS satellite data. The pipeline begins by sampling targets from the TESS catalog, extracting their light curves, and applying statistical tests to flag potential eclipsers. Candidates are then cross-checked against six major variable-star catalogs to exclude known objects. Those flagged as novel undergo an automated pixel-level check to confirm the signal originates from the target star itself rather than a nearby contaminant. So far, 107 candidates have passed this check across 0.8% of the TESS sky. The results are trustworthy because each candidate survives multiple independent vetting stages: statistical gates that measure eclipse depth and periodicity, novelty matching across established surveys, and automated pixel-level confirmation. The pipeline also compares odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses to catch potential period aliases. While this automated vetting is rigorous, candidates may carry open caveats noted on their individual pages, and further characterization beyond this pipeline's scope remains possible.
